topic: Agent Card Entitlements Guide 2026: Control Who Can Discover A2A Agents

competitors.title: A2A Protocol Specification v1.0.0 (Agent Discovery: The Agent Card)
key_points: Agent Card is the foundational discovery mechanism — a JSON metadata document published by each A2A Server describing identity, capabilities, skills, service endpoint, and authentication requirements
Section 8 defines two discovery mechanisms: well-known URI (/.well-known/agent.json) and registry-based discovery
Agent Card includes: name, description, url, version, capabilities (streaming, pushNotifications, extendedAgentCard), skills (with id, name, description, tags, examples), and securitySchemes
Section 13.3 Extended Agent Card Access Control: authenticated agents can access a more detailed card with additional skills/capabilities not in the public card
SecuritySchemes support APIKey, HTTPAuth, OAuth2 (authorization code, client credentials, device code), OpenIDConnect, and MutualTLS — enabling fine-grained entitlement enforcement
Extended Agent Card replaces cached public card for the duration of authenticated session — enabling runtime entitlement decisions based on client identity

competitors.title: Secure A2A Authentication with Auth0 and Google Cloud (2025)
key_points: Auth0 partnered with Google Cloud to define A2A authentication specs based on secure standards including OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
Agent Cards declare securitySchemes — clients authenticate using one of these schemes before they can access extended capabilities
CIBA (Client Initiated Backchannel Authentication) flow enables authentication for headless agents without browser UIs
Key enterprise auth questions for A2A: authentication, delegation, consent, authorization, headless agent auth, fine-grained permissions
Auth0's working sample demonstrates HR agent entitlement: only authenticated clients with valid scopes can discover and interact with the agent
Agent Cards can express scope requirements per skill — fine-grained entitlement beyond simple binary access

competitors.title: MCP vs A2A: A Guide to AI Agent Communication Protocols (Auth0)
key_points: Agent Cards serve as the discovery/trust mechanism before agents delegate work — 'self-descriptions that each agent publishes outlining what they can do, what protocols they speak, and what kind of requests they accept'
A2A roles: Client agents (initiate requests) and Remote/Service agents (advertise capabilities via Agent Cards)
Discovery flow: client agent reviews remote agents' cards to find the right collaborator for each subtask
Card contents intentionally limit information to avoid exposing sensitive implementation details — entitlement boundaries are built into the card model

competitors.title: Palo Alto Networks: A2A Protocol Security Analysis (via existing research synthesis)
key_points: Agent Card entitlements create a new attack surface: unauthorized agents could discover and interact with enterprise agents without proper authentication
Access-controlled discovery requires Agent Cards to have non-public components (Extended Agent Cards) gated behind authentication
Enterprise deployment pattern: public Agent Card with minimal capabilities for basic discovery, Extended Agent Card with full skill listing only after OAuth 2.0 authentication
Authorization scoping (Section 13.1 of spec): clients can only access tasks visible to their authenticated identity — same principle applies to Agent Card discovery

competitors.title: Google A2A Protocol: Multi-Agent Communication Guide (Atlan, 2026)
key_points: A2A compliance alone does not solve shared context, semantic alignment, or governance — entitlement policy must be handled separately
Agent Cards include authentication schemes (OAuth 2.0, API keys) to control which agents can discover and interact with each other
Discovery, authorization, and communication are the three pillars of A2A — entitlements cut across all three

stats.fact: A2A protocol v1.0.0 released by Linux Foundation in 2026 with 150+ supporting organizations including Google, Microsoft, AWS, Auth0, Atlan, and Palo Alto Networks
Agent Card is served at /.well-known/agent.json, following the established well-known URI pattern pioneered by ACME (RFC 8555), Apple App Site Association, and MCP Server Cards
Agent Cards support 5 security scheme types: APIKey, HTTPAuth, OAuth2 (with 3 flow variants), OpenIDConnect, and MutualTLS
Extended Agent Cards allow authenticated clients to access additional skills, capabilities, and configuration not available in public cards — creating the entitlement boundary
A2A H2 2026 roadmap includes authorization schemes in Agent Cards, dynamic skill querying, and dynamic UX negotiation inside tasks
stats.source: A2A Protocol GitHub project (via existing research)

stats.fact: Auth0 and Google Cloud partnered to define A2A auth specs with CIBA (Client Initiated Backchannel Authentication) for headless agent authentication
MCP Server Cards follow a parallel pattern at /.well-known/mcp.json with 75% of gateway vendors expected to integrate MCP features by end of 2026
ACP Agent Registry by JetBrains and Zed (Jan 2026) lists 30+ AI agents — a contrasting centralized registry model vs A2A's decentralized well-known URI approach to agent discovery
78% of enterprise AI teams (50+ AI/ML practitioners) report at least one MCP-backed agent in production as of Q1 2026, creating urgent need for cross-agent entitlement and discovery controls

The A2A spec defines Data Access and Authorization Scoping (Section 13.1) requiring that clients only access tasks visible to their authenticated identity — the same principle extends to Agent Card discovery
Agent Cards support AgentCardSignature for cryptographically signed cards, enabling verifiable identity for agent-to-agent trust without a central registry

angles: Public vs private Agent Cards: every A2A agent needs a public card, but enterprise agents should gate full capabilities behind Extended Agent Cards with OAuth 2.0 authentication
Entitlement as three-layer problem: (1) who can discover the agent exists, (2) who can see its full capabilities, (3) who can actually invoke its skills
The .well-known/agent.json pattern is the DNS of AI agents — treat it like an API contract with securitySchemes as first-class citizens
Agent Card signing enables decentralized trust: agents can verify each other's identity without a central registry, critical for cross-organization agent collaboration
CIBA flow solves the 'headless agent' auth problem for A2A: agents without UIs can authenticate users via push notification or out-of-band channels before granting access to restricted cards
Real-world comparison: MCP Server Cards (tool discovery) vs A2A Agent Cards (agent discovery) vs ACP Registry (editor-based agent registry) — each solves a different discovery problem
Enterprise Shadow Discovery risk: unregistered A2A agents with open Agent Cards bypass governance — enterprises need Agent Card registries with entitlement policy enforcement
The entitlement gap: A2A v1.0 spec defines how to declare auth schemes but does not mandate authorization enforcement — production systems must implement their own policy layer

Agent Cards become an enterprise control point: capability discovery, auth schemes, supported modalities, version negotiation, and policy metadata should be treated like API contracts with access controls
Recommended architecture: public Agent Card (minimal, discoverable) → Extended Agent Card (full skills, OAuth 2.0 gated) → In-Task Authorization (per-skill scope enforcement)
